What is the belief of atheists regarding the explanation of everything through science? Is there a possibility of something beyond explanation according to atheists? The question of what atheists believe about the explanation of everything through science can be a bit misleading. Many atheists aren't necessarily "believers" in science, so much as they see it as the only reliable tool we have for addressing objective issues. If you want to know about what truly happened in the past, for example, science is a better method of finding out than any other way of knowing such as anecdotes, feelings, philosophy, or religious revelation. And just to reiterate, that's why the term 'atheist' can be misleading, too. It is far more about what they don't believe than what they do. It’s not about what they believe; it's about what they *don't* believe. So, the answer to the question about a possibility of something beyond explanation largely depends on the specific issue. Atheists generally do not believe that there is anything *inherently* beyond explanation, but they fully understand that the current reach of science is limited. We don't know everything. The things we don't know, we are working on figuring out. And the fact that we are ignorant of certain knowledge doesn’t point to the existence of things *beyond* scientific explanation, but rather to the fact that we simply don’t know the answers, yet.

Atheists, isn't your Darwinian theory a little far-fetched when you think about it? The theory states that all living things have a common ancestor. An elephant and a mosquito share a common ancestor? Really? When I've talked to people about this, part of the misconception seems to be expecting something like a mosquito evolving into something like an elephant, or vice versa. But that's not the way evolution works. Both mosquitos and elephants are highly evolved, complex creatures. But their common ancestor wasn't anywhere near as complex as either of them. Take a look at the oldest known bilaterian animal (i.e. the group that includes elephants and mosquitos). This likely isn’t the actual, specific common ancestor, but it would have been fairly similar. SOURCE: Oldest “bilaterian” found: wormlike creature discovered along with its tracks From our modern point of view, that's a pretty simple, worm-like animal (though in its own time, it was one of the more complex creatures yet to evolve). But from that worm-like form, as it's descendants carried on and diversified, each separate lineage was free to 'add on' to that body plan, evolving into more complex forms as time went by. But since they were separate lineages, they couldn't share mutations between them. Each lineage went its own way, so that the types of complexity that evolved in each lineage was different from their cousin lineages. SOURCE: ResearchGate.net - Origin and Evolution of Nervous Systems As far as insects in particular, you can trace their evolutionary history, and see how various traits evolved generation by generation, eventually resulting in the complexity of modern day mosquitos: SOURCE: Fossils, genes and the evolution of animal limbs - Nature Likewise, you can trace the independent evolutionary history of vertebrates, which followed a different path, resulting in a different type of complex body plan: SOURCE: Fossils, genes and the evolution of animal limbs - Nature In fact, you can do this for the whole tree of life. The organisms we see today are the tips of the branches. The tips didn't evolve into the other tips. Instead, you have to trace the branches back in time to find the common ancestors that the branches evolved from. SOURCE: Researchgate.net - Informational Ecological and System Approaches for Complete Genome Analysis So, again, that’s how mosquitos and elephants evolved from a common ancestors. That ancient ancestor wasn’t yet very mosquito-like nor very elephant-like. It was really much more worm-like. It’s only as time went on, and each of those lineages went their separate ways, that one particular lineage evolved into mosquitos, while a different lineage evolved into elephants. And I can also add that it's worth repeating that, as an aside, all the normal caveats go here. Most Christians and other religious folks accept evolution, so this isn’t an atheist vs. religious issue. And most folks only use ‘Darwinian’ in a more historical context, specifically in reference to natural selection, to contrast with other ideas on evolution (like Lamarckian use and disuses). The modern day theory is the Modern Synthesis, which includes many more concepts and principles than Darwin ever knew about.

Do they still teach the myth about Columbus being the first European to reach the Americas in US schools? They don't teach that myth, but some schools might still teach other myths. One that still persists, even though it has been rejected by almost all serious researchers and historians, is the very idea of 'great men' in history. You know, like the 'great man' who 'invented' the lightbulb, the 'great man' that discovered gravity, and maybe one of the biggest myths out there, the 'great man' hero who supposedly invented the internet. It's very convenient that all of these 'great men' were white. I remember being taught this in my high school history classes, and it seemed like pretty much everyone was white, European, male, and the possessor of some divine insight. In reality, the lightbulb and internet, for example, were not just the idea of one person. The lightbulb went through decades of research, experiments, and improvements by various people, with the 'great man' just being the one who was the final popularizer. Likewise, the internet wasn't just 'invented' by one person. It was the result of a whole series of innovations that, over several decades, grew and expanded. Many of these 'great men' also didn’t accomplish particular achievements, on their own, at their own initiative. They were instead a product of the times, as well as benefitting from the work of other people, and most of the time were only getting ahead. However, the great man theory is an easy idea to sell. It's a simple narrative, in which a single person can be credited for all the good things that happened. It also conveniently aligns with a narrative that puts white men on top as the ones who deserve all the accolades. It's been rejected, by historians, as a simplification of reality, and as a vehicle for the glorification of certain people at the expense of others. But it still persists, especially in popular culture, which is, of course, where most people get a lot of their 'history' from.

Is it considered rude to be served on paper plates and plastic utensils at a dinner party? It depends on the formality of the party and the number of guests. But even then, there are other options besides paper plates. Say you're just having a casual event, a cookout of burgers and brats. Then fine, paper plates are adequate. But if you're going for something a little more upmarket, such as a sit-down dinner with several courses, maybe try some other options. If it's a small enough dinner party to where you own enough plates to cover it, go with real plates. And of course, real silverware. But if you just want to save yourself the cleanup, you might go for something a little classier than standard plastic. In fact if you really want to step it up, you could go with something like this: ABOVE SOURCE: Amazon.com Even if people are more relaxed about the dinnerware, they’re not going to complain about a party that's too successful. If a big party is being hosted, disposable dinnerware is really the only practical option. But a lot of people will take into account just how many guests you're expecting beforehand, so they can plan accordingly. And if you let people know beforehand, then people will adjust their expectations accordingly. Basically, just think about the formality of the event that you're trying to throw.

Are atheists truly correct if everything has to have a creator? The Earth can't come out of nothingness. It had to be created by something. If everything has to have a creator, then who created that creator? This is a question that's been asked by both believers and non-believers for ages. But even assuming some kind of intelligent design, who designed the designer? What made it create? There's no obvious place to just stop and say 'that's just the way things are' any more than there's a stopping point for explaining how the universe got started. It's a regress, and that's the central issue with the argument from design. However, there are arguments supporting that everything can come from nothing in areas of physics like quantum mechanics. A common one is that the universe is not static. It is constantly expanding, so something, like energy, is being created from nothing, just every second of every day. But that, too, is not a perfect answer. We can observe something that happened, but can't really understand how things are happening at the most fundamental level. Nonetheless, it doesn't really make sense to simply state that there is a creator, the creator just "is" and always was - because that's not much more helpful than saying everything just appeared one day, with no particular rhyme or reason. And, as it turns out, a God concept raises further questions. After all, what are the physical characteristics of this God? What is its mind like? Does it have any goals or desires? As a result, it tends to add complexity to the situation rather than eliminate it.

I have responded to a fare number of Christian trolls on here as a Christian myself, so this is an honest question. Regardless of which theistic religion, would there be anything that could convince you of the existence of a god(s)? If so, wouldn’t that make you more agnostic that truly atheist? (I believe the wisest amongst us are the agnostics) That’s a good question. I'd have to say that it depends on the evidence. If I were presented with definitive, verifiable, and irrefutable evidence of a god, I’d certainly reconsider my position. But what constitutes 'definitive' and 'irrefutable'? That's the tricky part. And, as I’m sure you already know, it's not a simple matter of miracles. People have claimed to witness miracles for millennia, and they've claimed to witness the miracles of every imaginable religion, but still fail to convince the majority of scientists, much less atheists. So what would convince an atheist? Well, I'd start with something simple: a repeatable, verifiable instance. Perhaps a god physically intervening in the physical world in a way that defied the known laws of physics. But that would just be a starting point. It also wouldn't be enough to prove it’s a god, in the sense that all human religions describe. To be sure, I would need far more information. Some way to be sure that I wasn’t being duped somehow, etc. But ultimately, the existence of a god is an empirical question. The more a god does, the easier it is to empirically study. And the more it does, and the more we can study that, the less likely it is that it’s an abstract notion of some kind. And to your more general question about the difference between atheism and agnosticism, I'm not sure it's a binary choice. You can be an agnostic atheist, or an agnostic theist. I identify now as an agnostic atheist. A strong, confident belief in non-belief, or that gods and/or the supernatural exist, can be intellectually dishonest.

So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat? They’re not. Not only does this run contrary to a massive body of evidence, but it’s not even what pilots themselves say. Pilots use a lot of scientific principles as part of their job, and understand basic physics. Even the curvature of the Earth is taken into account when charting a flight path. You can't just go from Point A to Point B in a straight line if the Earth is a sphere, particularly when traveling over longer distances. And yet, there are people who *claim* that pilots are saying that the Earth is flat, and thus should be trusted. But why would anyone trust the claims of people who are demonstrably wrong about what pilots are saying? As I said before, without evidence-based reasoning, methods are worthless at this task. The reality is that a very, very small percentage of pilots, if any, actually believe the Earth is flat. You can easily find instances of people claiming to be such, but their claims are easily debunked when they try to explain their "evidence”. I mean, a brief web search for "pilot flat earth" comes up with nothing but debunking videos and articles. So in the meantime, it's best to disregard such claims, regardless of how they are presented.

Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs? This supposed secret life of Jesus reeks of wishful thinking, a desire to salvage what one can after facing the inconvenient realities of historical and archeological evidence. Much like the claims of secret societies pulling the strings of the world, such fanciful notions are far easier to dream up than to prove. Consider how many people have to be “in on” such a conspiracy. The resurrection story involves many people, according to the Gospels. If Jesus truly survived, then this vast collection of co-conspirators would have to agree to lie about Jesus' existence, the manner of his death, and his resurrection. That’s a lot of people to lie and keep lied for centuries, without a single leak. A lone individual may maintain a secret, but not so many for so long. Given human nature and the chaotic nature of history, it is impossible to maintain such a long-lasting subterfuge. This tale, just like others, doesn't hold any water when subjected to even a modicum of critical inquiry, much less the rigorous testing of science. Instead, it falls apart under scrutiny, revealing more about the motivations and biases of those who originated and maintain these claims, rather than anything factual.

👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? Whether that's actually true is something that I'm not qualified to answer, although, in my opinion, there is a great deal of myth-making and storytelling involved. And I'd also say there are probably other motivations. For example, if you were a follower of Jesus during the first century, there would have been a lot of incentives to write about him. Those writings would have served as a way to spread his teachings and build a community. In a world of mostly non-literate people, the written word would have also given a specific group of people credibility and social standing. When it comes to religious texts, it’s generally pretty easy to find a common thread of an author attempting to inspire, teach, or persuade the reader of something, no matter how ridiculous. And when the reader buys into the author's teachings, it provides them with a sense of belonging and identity, therefore strengthening their faith. If you're looking for an objective account of the life of Jesus, the texts of the New Testament are probably not the best source because of those motivations.

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? I'm not a legal scholar, but I'm guessing the answer is 'no'. As long as the teacher isn't advocating for a particular religious viewpoint, she should be able to offer a truly balanced perspective on the subject. If she's merely pointing out the areas where the theory of evolution has some gaps and unanswered questions, she could be teaching perfectly acceptable science. Now, you've got to be careful here. There's a fine line between that and promoting a specific religious agenda. For example, I don't think it's appropriate for our biology teacher to say something like, "Well, the science just isn't there yet for how everything got started, but that's because God did it." That's obviously promoting a certain religious viewpoint. But she might be able to say something like, "While we know the basic framework of how species evolve over time, we still have some open questions about the origin of life and the conditions that allowed it to begin." That's just stating scientific fact, and it's still appropriate. It would go without saying that she shouldn’t give any undue weight to creationist arguments. In the same way that science courses shouldn't give any undue weight to astrology. It's pretty clear that creationism doesn't meet the standards of science. But in the interests of thoroughness, she may even be able to briefly mention creationism, but only to illustrate why it's not a legitimate scientific theory. It's tough to say exactly where the line is. But there's a wide range of possible scenarios, and it seems like many of them would be perfectly fine.

WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc? Frankly, I'm as eager as anyone to ditch the daily grind of congested commutes and the constant threat of automotive mishaps. When will we see sleek, automated vehicles effortlessly gliding through the air, transforming our daily lives into something out of a sci-fi flick? The reality is, the future isn’t a monolithic event, but a process with no defined start or end date. The technological underpinnings of these advances are, in many cases, already here. We have the tools, the materials of tomorrow, even to build the Judge Dredd sized buildings. What we lack is the widespread implementation and acceptance. The transition won’t be overnight. There will be a series of incremental steps, of failures and successes, that slowly nudge us closer to the vision of a futuristic utopia. It will be a marathon of incremental improvements instead of a sprint to a finished product. We have to learn how to address the inevitable hurdles. We have to consider the ethics of automation in transportation, and to build the regulatory framework to make sure that these technologies are used safely for the public. We have to make sure that the future is built on evidence-based reasoning, just like science. The future is more complex than an easy equation to solve.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? That’s a tough one. I could go back and forth, running through the various arguments. Depending on the day, you can find arguments for either side. For example, one of the biggest arguments that Donald Trump could lose is the sheer unpopularity of the man himself, or rather, of his political positions. He really does have a lot of baggage that’s hard, maybe even impossible, for him to shake off. Of course, there are plenty of arguments against Kamala Harris. For example, the economy, the crime rate, and a whole host of other issues that are currently going on could sink her. And any one particular event could swing the election one way or the other. The 2024 election is going to see a lot of mudslinging, and I don’t think it will be very pleasant to watch. No one knows for sure how the election will play out, but it will be very close. Just like in 2020, the election probably will depend on the swing states, and it could be a very long night before we know the final results. Of course, you do have plenty of other candidates running for president, too. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Marianne Williamson are two of the most prominent third-party candidates seeking the presidency. But neither is likely to be elected. They might make things more difficult for the two main candidates, but that’s about it. And that’s not even taking into account any potential third-party candidates in the future either. So honestly, I don’t know who would win the election. But one thing’s for sure: it will be highly contested and will be sure to be quite a spectacle.

What is the probability that a satellite the size of the moon, would orbit just the right distance from a planet the size of the earth, that from the planet, it appears the same size as a star the size of the sun, at its distance from that planet? That's a fun question, and it helps bring home the importance of luck in our own story. It requires a bit of math that I'm not going to go into right now, but the answer is incredibly low. But it's also worth noting that the 'moon' is a lot smaller than either the Earth or the sun. So while the probability is still incredibly small, it's worth breaking it down into smaller parts. We can think of it in a few different ways, and each breaks down even further. When you get to the issue of size, it's a question of how the light from the sun travels across space. The brightness decreases with the square of the distance. And the size of the object is also similarly affected by the square of the distance. So, you have to 'get lucky' in terms of the ratio between a planet and moon, and also the ratio between those relative sizes and the sun's size and distance. That's just a handful of the huge number of separate issues involved in even just those 'simple' questions. Then you have other issues as well, like the orbital speed of the moon, the eccentricity of the orbit, the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to the sun, the luminosity of the sun, and also how the sun's luminosity changes both gradually over time, and in flare ups. Basically, anything that effects the relative amounts of sunlight that hit the satellite versus planet. And if you think about the total range of planets and moons you might observe in our galaxy, and think about what conditions are required for life, then our galaxy is only a tiny fraction of the observable universe. And if you think about all the potential universes in the multiverse, then the chance of a planet like Earth having a moon, and being in a position where it could host life, seem even more astronomically low. It's hard to say how low those odds are, especially since we don't know what the multiverse is actually like. But when you add it up, it makes our own history seem even more mind-boggling.

If the weight of a body in water is 12N and weight of liquid displaced by the body is 8N, then what is the weights of that object in air? This is a straightforward physics problem, making it quite unlike many other questions people ask. And by all means, physics problems aren't hard. You just need to understand the concepts. Here's the important concept to understand: The buoyant force is equal to the weight of the liquid displaced. In this case, the buoyant force is 8N. You can also think of the buoyant force as the amount by which the object appears to weigh less in water as opposed to in air. So, the weight of the object in water is 12N, but in air, the object weighs more. Now, what's the difference between an object's weight in air and its weight in water? It's the buoyant force. If the weight of the object in water is 12N, and the buoyant force is 8N, what is the weight of the object in air? Simple subtraction will do the trick: you just add the buoyant force to the weight of the object in water (12N + 8N = 20N). Therefore, the object weighs 20N in air. Pretty simple, eh? You'd think it'd be more complicated, but that's the elegance of physics: even when issues *are* complex, the relationships between forces and interactions are often relatively simple.

Why are millenial and gen Z women so much likelier to wait until their 30s to settle down and are far more sleighted to want to sleep around with tens of people before earnestly looking for a partner? No shame, no blame. Just curious. There's a lot of discussion about this, as a matter of fact. Several factors are at play, and it's a bit complex to pinpoint one specific reason. One major contributing factor appears to be a shifting economic landscape. Millennials and Gen Z entered adulthood during periods of economic instability and uncertainty. Many faced significant student loan debt, a tougher job market, and higher housing costs. This financial strain often leads to delaying major life decisions, including marriage and having children. SOURCE: The Economic Landscape for Millennial and Gen Z Women. Another important aspect is changing social norms. There's been a significant cultural shift away from the pressure to get married young. Marriage is no longer seen as the only path to fulfillment, and there's increased acceptance of various lifestyles, including cohabitation, singlehood, and prioritizing career goals. These shifts have changed the social expectations and timeline of traditional partnerships. SOURCE: The Changing Social Norms of Women in the 21st Century. Advancements in reproductive technology also play a major role. Women now have more control over their reproductive choices, including delaying childbearing through contraception and assisted reproductive technologies like egg freezing. This offers more flexibility in planning their lives and prioritizing career goals or personal growth without the pressure of biological limitations. SOURCE: Technological Advancements in Women’s Reproductive Health. Moreover, higher levels of education for women are correlated with delaying marriage. Women with higher levels of education often spend more time in school and establishing their careers before settling down. This leads to a greater emphasis on financial independence and career achievement as a precursor to marriage. SOURCE: The Impact of Educational Attainment on Marriage Timing Among Women. Of course, it's all a complex interplay of choices. It's less about a particular group being 'likelier' to do something and more about broader societal shifts and personal preferences that have opened up a larger range of options. It's not really a matter of morality, but a natural consequence of a dynamic society.

Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how? That’s a significant question, and it gets even more philosophically complicated when you consider what “better” actually means. For example, scientists can manipulate genes, and often do, to give a particular breed of, say, dog, specific traits. Often, this is to fulfill the desires of pet owners. So, is that making life better? For those owners, perhaps. For the dog? Maybe. But it could be that in the long run, the dog’s genetic modifications lead to a shorter lifespan than it otherwise might have. SOURCE: The Genetics of Dog Breeding | VCA Animal Hospitals That’s more often the case than not, since there's a reason why most dog breeds are unhealthy: there are too few members of their species to maintain the population’s health. Humans have intervened with the dog’s genome, through selective breeding, to give them more human-centric qualities at the cost of their biological health. Consider how you want a dog to behave in your house, as opposed to how likely that dog is to live a long, healthy life. One of those will win out over the other. In fact, there's a great argument to be made that dogs would be much better off in an evolutionary sense if humans were not involved in their evolutionary development at all. Just a random thought of mine. As for the question of redefining or redesigning life, the answer is a definitive yes. Scientists are doing both, and even if they weren't intentionally, they’re making the same impact. For all the advancements we've made, there are still countless questions to be answered about the very concept of life.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I used to have a great, and indeed, frequent, neighbor who was as devout in his faith as I was in my engineering work. We had many friendly debates about religion, and honestly, he was one of the smartest, most well-read people I’ve ever known. He could cite scripture and philosophy and science and history like nobody’s business, and he had an exceptional ability to make his arguments very clear. And that's the rub, in the end. Clarity doesn't make an argument right. Even he would admit that his particular interpretation of scripture had some shortcomings. But for the life of me, I can't remember him ever making truly compelling arguments in favor of actual, literal, young-Earth creationism. Perhaps he just didn't want to alienate me, but I never heard him make those kinds of arguments. The reason why is because, well, those arguments don't stand up to science. And if someone truly understands how science works, they're going to understand that, and they're going to be hesitant to argue against it. And as I mentioned before, science is the best tool we humans have for understanding objective issues. You can define "intelligent" any way you like, and certainly some people could probably fit the definition given some parameters. But in the end, it really depends on what parameters you use.

How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight? That depends on how much weight you're trying to lose, and what your diet looks like. If you eat a lot of unhealthy food, and/or simply eat too much food, then lots of exercise might be needed just to maintain. If you eat a fairly healthy diet and watch your calorie intake, then it might not take all that much exercise to lose weight. Of course, I'm not a health professional, so you might want the advice of a doctor, dietician, etc. In general, as far as a weight-loss program, I tend to see at least two basic approaches. And, just to be clear, I'm not advocating for either, here. I've just observed that these are the two most talked about: The first approach is to focus on calories. You need to burn more calories than you take in. If you're eating a lot of calories, then you need to either exercise more, or eat less. Or both. The second is to focus on macros and the types of foods you eat, like keto, paleo, etc. Some of these approaches focus on burning fat, rather than focusing on calories. Again, I'm not saying that one approach is better than the other. Both approaches have had their fair share of success stories and horror stories. But, I would say it's very difficult to lose weight and keep it off without both a calorie and a macro focus. And I'm not saying a calorie-focused or macro-focused approach *has to* be difficult, either. But it is a long-term lifestyle change, not a quick fix. And there’s plenty of misleading marketing, which can make the whole process extra difficult. For example, there are tons of weight loss supplements on the market with limited scientific backing. Many of these supplements prey on the desire for a quick fix. Just, stick to the basics: eat a healthy diet, exercise regularly, and make gradual changes. Don't make any drastic changes, and you'll be able to stick to it longer.

Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? No, there aren't. And in fact, that's not the way evolution works, either. The last thing that evolution ever "decides" is what to do. Evolution doesn't have a plan. Animals don't "decide" to evolve into another species. Instead, over millions of years, they have offspring. Some of those offspring have mutations that give them a slight advantage in their environment. The more offspring that have the same advantageous mutations, the larger that percentage in the population becomes. That advantage doesn't have to be particularly pronounced, either. A slight advantage will be sufficient in a given environment, over enough time, to radically change the population, generation by generation. And just to harp on this point one more time, "walking onto land" isn't literally that, either. The first animals that became capable of living on land did so in stages. There isn't some one single fish that decided to just start walking around. They were fish that could survive at the water's edge a little bit longer than the other fish. And over millions of years, with different random mutations, little by little, they became amphibians. And, as I mentioned before, here's the deal - the fossils don't magically appear by themselves. Paleontologists have to spend lots of time and effort finding and identifying them. Even after that discovery, it still needs to become part of the public discourse. Sometimes the relevant fossils have only been described in academic papers read by just a handful of people. But there certainly has been a lot of work done on this, and we do have a pretty good idea: SOURCE: New Fossils Provide Evidence of the Fish-Tetrapod Transition In the evolutionary history, it wasn't like there was fish and humans. It was, as with all evolution, a gradual process, with plenty of intermediate species. One example is Tiktaalik roseae, which is a well known transitional fossil. Tiktaalik had fins, but also had features that would let it push up from the ground. As such, it's known as a "fishapod". Source: Wikipedia.com. There were earlier fossil fish like Panderichthys, and later on, there were the fully formed tetrapods like Acanthostega. Now, I admit, I'm simplifying a bit here, since, in general, evolutionary paleontological papers are more interesting. But for clarity's sake, you can imagine these sorts of transitions as, perhaps, being steps of a ladder. At the bottom rung, you have fish, with the tetrapods at the top. The "fishapods" are somewhere in the middle. But I digress.

Is Terrence Howard right that 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 x 1 = 2? No, Terrence Howard isn't right. He's making stuff up to sound smart. 1 + 0 = 1 in all the math systems that anyone actually uses. And 1 x 1 = 1. When mathematicians or scientists are trying to be sure that their ideas are valid, they try to make them verifiable to be sure that they're right. The standards of science are evidence based reasoning, peer review, and reproducibility. You can show me the evidence that Howard is right, and maybe I’d re-evaluate my opinion. Though, I kind of doubt it. It actually sounds like Howard is doing the exact opposite by saying 1 x 1 = 2. But, again, give me some evidence of this if you can. I assume he's attempting to get some kind of "deep" insight in the realm of advanced math. But I'm afraid that he's just trying to impress the ladies. If your idea of "deep" is just making up whatever you feel like, then you'll get all kinds of weird results that don't really make any sense. You can start out with assumptions that aren't correct, and then reach any conclusions you want. It's like a child’s game in a way. Sure, you can pretend to make it make sense if you'd like. But, if you're not using evidence based reasoning, you're not actually adding to humanity's knowledge. It helps to have your arguments pass the test of 'reality'. That's why good science isn't really a way to 'think'. It's a way to check your thinking. If you're working in a field where you need to make sure that things are really, actually correct, like aerospace engineering or medicine, you can't be making stuff up. You have to present a rigorous case for why your ideas are correct. And then you have to be open enough to admit that you're wrong if the evidence isn't there. That's why Terrence Howard, at least in this case, is wrong.

Why do people seem to think gun control laws matter when in reality if I want to obtain a gun and the government thought it could stop me, I'd just obtain a gun through illegal means? Well, it's not that simple. I think people often underestimate the real effect of gun control, even if they're right that it can't absolutely stop every bad actor from obtaining a firearm. The truth is, we don't know what the exact effect of any gun control law will be. It only makes intellectual sense to assume that reducing the overall number of guns available to the public will reduce gun violence. The question mark is how and by how much. Consider the many different types of gun violence that exist. Some, like mass shootings, are relatively rare, but they get the most media coverage, and thus the most legislative attention. Other types of gun violence, like suicides, are far more common, and the type of gun control law that might prevent it will be different. Still, there is also no question that a lot of the gun violence is due to the illicit availability of firearms used in crimes. No one would dispute the idea that any gun control law aimed at this type of firearm should have a real impact, by further restricting their availability. After all, that's why you have these laws in the first place, even if they're not always a complete success. It's a little like how we try to prevent illegal drugs from entering the US. No one thinks we'll be able to stop every drug that comes across the border but it keeps some percentage of them out. A sensible approach would be to implement a set of gun laws to prevent different types of access, tailored to the types of problems those gun control laws would be addressing, such as by restricting certain types of firearms. And, like any science, you need to keep gathering evidence and rethinking the approach to make it work better.

Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Do they have an urge to climb trees? Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? Okay, so the whole monkeys thing is a straw man, a simplistic misrepresentation that atheists are somehow denying or disavowing their humanity. It completely misses the point of atheism, which boils down to not believing in gods. Not believing in gods doesn’t mean you think you're an ape. Anyone who presents it like that either doesn't understand the issue or is deliberately trying to misrepresent the idea. As for climbing trees, that's just silly. Sure, humans are primates, and primates are adapted to climb, but so are a lot of other life forms, and it has nothing to do with belief or disbelief. The whole idea is ridiculous. As for whether it's sad to believe in oneself, well, it depends on what that means, doesn't it? Believing in yourself, in the sense of having self-confidence and self-respect, is generally a good thing. It can help you overcome challenges and achieve your goals. But if you're suggesting some kind of narcissism, that's probably not the best way to live. It's possible to have both a healthy level of self-belief and also recognize your flaws and the strengths of other people. Believing in one's self to the exclusion of all else, that sounds a bit lonely to me. And, it could very well lead to all manner of problems.

Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs? The answer to that is even more complicated than the evolution of mosquitos and elephants. In this case, we aren't just talking about all life. We are talking about the animals that wound up being the ancestors of humans. The vast majority of creatures on Earth are invertebrates, but humans have the characteristic of being vertebrates. That means we are animals with spines, and who used to live in the water. So, there is a long line of aquatic animals that evolved into the first land vertebrates, known as tetrapods, which means "four feet." The first tetrapods were the descendants of the lobe-finned fishes. They lived during the late Devonian period, around 375 million years ago. One of the best-known fossils of the tetrapod group is Tiktaalik roseae, pictured below. SOURCE: Tiktaalik roseae - Wikipedia The Tiktaalik roseae probably wasn't the specific creature that all tetrapods evolved from. But it was very close. It had a lot of tetrapod-like features: ribs, a neck, and limb-like fins. But it also had some fish-like features, like scales and fins. Its closest relative may have been the earlier, more fish-like Elpistostege, which was discovered even earlier than Tiktaalik roseae, so the true ancestor might yet be found. In any case, this evolutionary progression of aquatic to land animals had to get around a lot of problems. Fish have gills that get oxygen from the water. But gills don't work in the air. Land animals need lungs for their oxygen. They also need limbs that can support their weight. Fish, of course, have neither.

Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"? I think there's some truth to that. I’m not sure if America's in the worst shape it's ever been, but even if it isn’t, it's not exactly in terrific shape either. It's also certainly true that every civilization through history has had a sizable portion of people who aren't overly concerned with intellectual pursuits. And to be clear, I don’t mean every single person has to be a rocket scientist or read Plato in the original Greek. We all have lives to live, and there are plenty of valid reasons for not spending a lot of time on intellectual endeavors. But when a sizable percentage of the population is actively hostile to intellectualism, that's a different story. And that’s exactly the kind of problem that societies have faced throughout human history. As far back as the ancient Greeks, philosophers and scientists had to deal with an anti-intellectual sentiment that was already well-established. This wasn't even an exclusively problem in any particular democracy vs. oligarchy or whatever governmental system either. Even some of history's most enlightened leaders had to deal with the problem. But those were simpler times. Today, we have the Internet and easily accessed misinformation and disinformation campaigns run by foreign/domestic bad actors with a goal in mind. And there are plenty of folks out there who are just eating up the lies.

Question for atheists- how do you feel about Christians talking about their faith with you if they are nice about it (ie not screaming that you are going to Hell)? Do Christians in this manner bother you? I hope my question makes sense. It's not something that bothers me *per se*, no. I mean, they're just talking about what they believe. And I'm not sitting there fuming, or getting all huffy. If they're not being jerks, which it sounds like your assumption is they aren't, it's no big deal. Now, I am somewhat skeptical about how effective such discussions can be, and I've got a feeling it's a two-way street. I don't think I'm going to 'convert' to their way of thinking. They're probably not going to 'convert' to mine. But, for that matter, people in general are resistant to changing their mind to *any* new information. Just because somebody disagrees with you, doesn’t necessarily mean they haven’t given thought to the matter. I mean, for the most part, it's not really that big a deal. They're just trying to share what they believe. The only exception is if they try to act like it is based on evidence or something, when that's just not the case. But even then, I'm not going to get all steamed up. Unless somebody is being actively harmful, which, again, it sounds like your question isn't about, there's no real reason to get all bent out of shape over it. And, to be sure, there might even be some moral lessons to be gleaned from the discussions, or at the very least, it's a learning experience in better understanding other people.

You say that Darwin proved we are all animals, but animals rarely practice birthcontrol, then why you do? The premise of the question is a bit off, I think. Darwin didn’t set out to ‘prove’ that we are all animals. That was one of the logical conclusions of his theories, but the goal of *On the Origin of Species* was figuring out the mechanics of evolution. And to answer your question, the practice of birth control isn't that complex. Humans take advantage of their higher level of intelligence, and their ability to modify their environment, to change their breeding patterns. So many different animals are able to exercise some level of control over their breeding habits. For example, in captivity, there is artificial insemination, and selective breeding based on desired traits. In the wild, various animals will leave their territories, or even kill their young to avoid overpopulation. But the real point I’d make is that these are minor modifications on top of a bigger point: birth control isn't always necessary. Plenty of animals don't have a very big percentage of fertile offspring, or suffer high infant mortality. And for those types of animals, or in those environments, there’s little evolutionary pressure to invent birth control. Also, it’s worth asking: what does ‘control’ mean? Humans can use birth control to have no kids. But humans also want to have kids, and they want to maximize their chances of having kids. Human beings have the ability to ‘control’ when it is best to have children.

Is it better to fly two long haul flights (say 10 hours each) instead of one ultra-long haul flight (about 18-19 hours)? It depends on the context. If you're mainly concerned about getting from Point A to Point B as quickly as possible, then you'd lean towards the ultra-long haul flight. You'd spend a little less time in transit. But then you have to consider everything else that goes along with that. Those ultra-long haul flights can be rough. You're squished into a chair for nearly a full day, dealing with the same recirculated air and the same noisy strangers. And if you're used to getting up and stretching your legs, you're not going to have as many opportunities to do that. You can try to take advantage of the airplane’s bathroom, but the aisles are usually pretty cramped, and it’s still not the same as walking around on solid ground. Plus, you’d be subjected to the same in-flight entertainment for the whole flight. So many movies and TV shows, no matter how good they are, can get repetitive after a while. There’s also the issue of flight delays. If one of the flights is delayed, there's no guarantee that the second flight will accommodate the change. So you'd be standing at the airport for a long time, probably without any good food or comfortable seating. On the other hand, two shorter flights can offer more flexibility. You have the possibility of better in-flight entertainment; you have a better chance of stretching your legs, and changing the ambient air. You also get to experience two different airports and the novelty of dealing with the airport staff twice and navigating two very different environments. So while an ultra-long haul flight might seem better in theory, the reality is more nuanced. If you're really worried about the duration of the journey, consider the impact on your well-being and whether or not the added time in transit balances with an overall better experience.

As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books? Absolutely. First off, let’s clarify what we mean by ‘perfectly accurate English.’ Are we talking about proper grammar, spelling, and lexicon as taught in school, or something more? If it's the former, then no, it’s not always necessary, or even desirable.  There are a whole host of situations where less-than-perfect grammar and usage are appropriate. A few examples of these situations are:  *   **Context:** If speaking to small children, or people learning English, you often have to simplify your language. You wouldn't want to give an advanced lecture to a toddler. *   **Dialect, Slang, & Other Idioms:** If you’re trying to fit into a specific culture, then using colloquial English or even another language entirely is the best way to be understood and accepted. Similarly, various subcultures might involve specialized vocabulary, so you might need to do the same. *   **Artistic Expression:** Creative writing, acting, music, etc., frequently involve deliberately breaking grammatical rules to create certain effects. Punctuation too. Think about the use of stream-of-consciousness in novels, or certain musical choices that deliberately stray from the norm. *   **Communicating Effectively:** Sometimes, the best way to communicate is a little vague. As an example, sarcasm and humor can require breaking of the rules.  Of course, I'm not advocating for the abandonment of proper English. It’s still critically important for clear communication and to be understood by the widest possible audience. But, if you are trying to be understood by a much smaller audience then the rules are there simply to inform you of what to do. They are not commands. And it’s not enough to just know the rules, you also have to know when to break them.

Should creationism be taught in public schools as an alternative to evolution, given its religious roots, or does doing so infringe upon the separation of church and state? This is a complex issue that's been fought in courtrooms for decades. The core argument is simple: public schools are funded by everyone, including people who may not share the same religious beliefs. Teaching creationism, which posits a supernatural explanation for the origin of the universe and life, would essentially be promoting a specific religious viewpoint. That's where the separation of church and state comes in; the government shouldn't be endorsing any particular religion. It would be like the school mandating prayer or displaying religious symbols in the classroom, which would likely be illegal in the U.S. Even if the school presented creationism as just *one* possible theory among several, it still runs into problems. The scientific consensus overwhelmingly supports evolution. Dismissing *that* theory in favor of an explicitly religious one is a misrepresentation of the scientific method. There's a huge difference between teaching students *about* different religions, which is valuable for cultural understanding, and advocating for a religious viewpoint as scientific fact. The former promotes critical thinking and understanding; the latter promotes religious indoctrination and potentially undermines scientific literacy.

Is music at best better than food? That's an interesting question. I'd have to say it depends on the music and the food. It's like asking if a good book is better than a good movie. Both can be enjoyable, and both are completely different experiences. If you're starving, food has a clear advantage. You need food to live, and the best music isn't going to help with that. But if you're not hungry, a really moving piece of music can be a more profound experience than a meal, no matter how good the meal is. Think of a specific concert, or a live performance. The experience is communal, and something that you can’t get just listening to a recording later. Of course, it depends on the type of music you listen to. Somebody who listens to nothing but polka music could have a different opinion than somebody who’s into classical. A country fan might disagree with a heavy metal fan. And different people will react to different genres or musical styles differently. There's also the issue of time. You can listen to a piece of music over and over. You can certainly eat a delicious meal over and over, but each meal is a unique experience that is gone forever. It’s harder to replicate the pleasure of a really fulfilling musical experience again and again. So, in the end, both food and music have their own strengths and weaknesses. They both serve different purposes, and elicit different emotions. Ultimately, it comes down to personal preference.
